The matter of the xièzhì (觟䚦) is simply a repeat of the stories of the fù qū yì (復屈軼).
Sheep originally have two horns.
The xièzhì (觟䚦) has one horn.
Its body is inferior to the group,
not as good as the many species.
How can it be considered wondrous?
A three-legged turtle is called néng (能).
A three-legged tortoise is called bì (賁).
According to this, néng (能) and bì (賁) are not as spiritually capable as four-legged turtles and tortoises.
How can a one-horned sheep be holier than two-horned animals?
The xīngxīng (狌狌) knows what is past.
The gānquè (乾鵲) knows what is to come.
Parrots and magpies can speak.
Natural ability enables them to do one thing,
but not two.
Perhaps the nature of the xièzhì (觟䚦) only allows it to butt people.
It may not necessarily know who is guilty.
Gāoyáo (皋陶) wished to use spiritual matters to aid governance.
He disliked that those who received punishment were not completely convinced [of their guilt].
Therefore, he made it so that if the xièzhì (觟䚦) butted someone, that person was guilty.
He wanted people to fear it and not commit crimes.
So that the families of those punished
would have no complaints even until death.
The nature of things is that each has its own knowledge.
If the xièzhì (觟䚦)'s ability to butt is called spiritual,
then the xīngxīng (狌狌) and others
are all spiritual.
Wū know good fortune and ill fortune,
predict people's misfortune and happiness,
and there is nothing that is not so.
If we consider *xièzhì* to be a type of *wū*,
then what is so remarkable about *wū* that we consider them good?
These are all instances of human desires using spiritual matters to establish transformations.
Shī Shàngfù was the Sīmǎ of Zhōu,
leading troops to attack Zhòu.
Arriving above the Méngjīn ford,
holding an axe and grasping the banner,
he called out to his troops, saying:
"Cāngsì!
Cāngsì!"
Cāngsì are,
water-dwelling beasts,
skilled at overturning people's boats.
Using spirits to transform,
he wanted to make them cross quickly,
saying that if they did not cross quickly,
the *cāngsì* would harm them,
which is similar to the *xièzhì*.
There is such a strange creature in the river,
sometimes appearing and floating,
with one body and nine heads.
People fear and detest it,
but it may not actually overturn people's boats.
Shàngfù relied on this strange creature in the river,
Therefore, it was used to awe the masses.
Now, the *xièzhì*'s 角 (jiǎo, horn) touching (or butting) criminals
is like a granary rhinoceros (*cāng sì*) overturning a boat;
it likely has a hollow reputation
without any real effectiveness.
People fear the strange and wondrous,
so they empty praise and embellish.
Furthermore, they say that in times of great peace, there are auspicious stars (*jǐng xīng*).
The *Shàngshū Zhōnghòu* says:
"During the time of Yáo, an auspicious star appeared in Zhěn."
Now, auspicious stars
are sometimes the five planets.
The larger ones
are Jupiter (Suìxīng),
and Venus (Tàibái).
Perhaps Jupiter
or Venus traveled through the constellation Zhěn.
The ancients were unsophisticated and unable to calculate the movements of the five planets.
They didn't know what Jupiter
or Venus looked like.
Seeing a large star, they called it an auspicious star.
The *Shī* (Book of Odes) also says:
"In the east, there is Qǐmíng,
in the west, there is Chánggēng."
It is also perhaps Jupiter
It is Venus.
Sometimes it is seen in the west at dusk,
sometimes it appears in the east at dawn.
If poets do not know this,
then they call it Qǐmíng,
or Cháng Gēng.
Therefore, Cháng Gēng is the same as Jǐng Xīng,
both being one of the five planets.
In times of great peace,
the sun and moon shine brightly.
The five planets
are similar to the sun and moon.
If in times of great peace there is already Jǐng Xīng,
can there then also be sun and moon?
Poets
are common people;
the time of "Zhōng Hòu",
an unsophisticated era,
all do not know the stars.
During the time of Wáng Mǎng,
Venus crossed the sky,
shining like a half moon,
if those who didn't know the stars saw it,
then they would also call it Jǐng Xīng.
The "Ěr Yǎ‧Shì Sì Shí Zhāng" says:
"Spring is for sprouting,
summer is for growing,
Autumn is for harvest,
winter is for peace and quiet.
The harmony of the four seasons is called "auspicious star".
As the "Ěryǎ" says,
"auspicious star" is a name for the harmonious combination of the four seasons,
I fear it is not a large star visible in the sky.
The book "Ěryǎ",
and the explanations of the Five Classics,
are what scholars commonly observe,
but they do not believe and follow it,
and instead call a large star an "auspicious star,"
is the "auspicious star" spoken of in the "Ěryǎ"
different from what scholars say?
The "Ěryǎ" also says:
"Sweet dew descends seasonally,
all things prosper,
it is called 'sweet spring'."
"Sweet spring" refers to sweet dew.
Now scholars explain it,
saying that a spring comes out from the ground,
its taste as sweet as sweet wine,
therefore it is called "sweet spring."
The two explanations are far apart,
and the truth is not yet known.
According to the "Ěryǎ‧Explanation of Water (
Spring) Chapter":
"A spring that appears and disappears is called jiān."
Kǎn Quán is directly flowing out.
"Zhèng chū"
means "gushing out."
Wò Quán hangs and flows out.
"Xuán chū"
means "flowing downwards."
These are different ways a spring emerges,
and each has a different name.
If, in a time of great peace,
there were truly a lì quán (sweet spring) emerging from the ground,
it should be discussed in this chapter.
Why is it instead placed in the "Shì Sì Shí Zhāng" (Explanation of the Four Seasons) chapter,
saying that sweet dew is lì quán?
If this is the case,
the Confucian scholars' saying that lì quán comes from the ground
and that sweet dew has a very sweet taste
is not reliable.
A Confucian scholar says:
"When the Dao reaches Heaven,
the sun and moon are brilliantly clear,
the stars do not lose their course,
a gentle wind rises,
and sweet rain falls."
Rain that clears after a period of gloom is called "sweet rain;"
it does not mean that the taste of the rainwater is sweet.
By this analogy,
"sweet dew" must refer to the time of its descent,
It appropriately nourishes the myriad things,
but it does not necessarily reveal a sweet taste.
There is also dew that reveals a sweet taste like candy or honey,
both being responses to great peace,
but not the sweet dew that nourishes the myriad things.
How can this be clarified?
Considering that the sweet dew that tastes like candy or honey
settles on trees,
not on the five grains.
The dew that does not taste sweet,
when it descends,
the land is moistened and flows with dampness,
and the myriad things are thoroughly moistened and saturated.
From this perspective,
the *Ěr Yǎ* is perhaps closer to the truth.
Based on the words of the *Ěr Yǎ*,
and verifying it with things,
considering that the sweet-tasting dew descends and settles on trees,
and observing the trees it settles on,
they do not flourish more than the trees it does not settle on.
Therefore, the sweet dew of today
is likely different from what the *Ěr Yǎ* calls sweet dew.
To verify the sweet dew of the *Ěr Yǎ*,
look for the flourishing and ripening of the myriad things,
and the absence of disasters;
this is the verification of the descent of sweet dew.
When sweet dew descends,
then there are sweet springs.
"Zhì Qí Piān" (Chapter on Governing by Time)
The world says that ancient rulers were wise,
therefore morality and virtue were practiced,
and when practiced, achievements were made and peace reigned;
if rulers were unworthy,
then morality and virtue were immediately abandoned,
and when abandoned, achievements were ruined and governance was chaotic.
Those who discuss this from ancient to modern times
would say that it is so.
Why?
They see Yáo
and Shùn as wise sages who brought about great peace,
Jié, Zhòu, being without the Dao, brought about chaos and were justly punished.
Speaking truthfully,
their lifespans were naturally determined,
not a matter of the power of virtue and transformation.
Officials of even a hundred *shí*
or even those receiving only a *dǒu* of grain,
residing in their positions and governing the people,
administering the government and disseminating teachings,
whether the teachings are practiced or cease,
whether the people are governed well or descend into chaos,
all of this is governed by fate.
Some are talented and of pure conduct,
yet their official positions remain vacant;
others are of shallow wisdom and base character,
yet they govern the people and gain position.
The ancient practice of promotion and demotion, obscure or manifest,
was to assess merit,
bestowing rewards based on demonstrated accomplishments
and administering punishments based on lack of accomplishment.
This assesses fate and increases emoluments,
not truly recognizing talent and greatly rewarding ability.
Those who discuss matters use the method of assessing merit,
basing their judgment of worth on observed results,
and therefore say that when the people are governed well and the state is secure,
it is brought about by a worthy ruler;
when the people are in chaos and the state is endangered,
it is brought about by a ruler without the Dao.
Therefore, when the change of danger and chaos arrives,
Those who criticize rulers
attribute the blame to the government's failure to follow the correct path.
The ruler accepts this criticism and blames himself,
filled with worry and deep thought,
affecting his physical well-being.
Yet the dangers and chaos
ultimately do not diminish.
This only stirs up resentment in the ruler's heart,
causing even the most insightful ruler
to unjustly bear the blame.
Public opinion spreads these claims,
causing them to be believed.
A wise ruler can govern a people who are destined for peace,
but cannot transform a world destined for chaos.
A skilled doctor can administer acupuncture and medicine,
and when the methods prove effective,
it is because they encountered someone who was not fated to die and a disease that was not fated to be fatal.
But if fate has run out and the illness is incurable,
then even *Biǎn Què* would be helpless.
The incurability of a life at its end and an incurable illness
is like the impossibility of pacifying a people destined for chaos;
the healing power of medicine
is like the pacifying power of education.
All these things have a destined time;
it is impossible to force them through effort.
*Gōng Bó Liáo* slandered *Zǐ Lù* to *Jì Sūn*,
and *Zǐ Fú Jǐng Bó* told *Kǒngzǐ* about it.
Confucius said:
"That the Way is about to be practiced,
it is fate!
That the Way is about to be abandoned,
it is fate!"
From this it can be said,
the practice and abandonment of teachings,
the peace and danger of a state,
all lie in fate and time,
not human effort.
Now, in times of chaos and rebellious people,
the state is in danger,
disasters are tied to Heaven,
the virtue of a virtuous ruler
cannot eliminate them.
The *Book of Poetry* speaks of King Zhōu Xuān suffering a great drought.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"The remaining people of Zhōu,
none were left remaining."
Saying that there was not a single person left who was not harmed.
King Xuān was virtuous,
but was suspected of having insufficient virtue;
as for those whose benevolence and kindness were greatest,
none surpassed Yáo and
Tāng. Yáo encountered a great flood,
Tāng encountered a great drought.
Floods and droughts
This is the most severe of disasters.
Yet, the two sages encountered them.
Could it be that these disasters were caused by the governance of the two sages?
It is the natural course of the cycles of Heaven and Earth.
Considering the floods and droughts of Yáo
and Tāng,
and comparing them to the disasters of all the kings,
they were not caused by governance.
If they were not caused by governance,
then blessings and aid
are not brought about by virtue.
A wise ruler governing a country
is like a loving father managing his household.
A loving father is patient in teaching, clarifies orders and decrees,
but cannot ensure that all his children and grandchildren will be filial and virtuous.
If the children and grandchildren are filial and virtuous,
the family prospers;
if the people are peaceful,
the country flourishes.
Prosperity must be followed by decline,
and flourishing by decay.
Flourishing and prosperity are not achieved through virtue,
then decline and decay are not caused by a lack of virtue.
Prosperity, decline, flourishing, and decay
are all due to the timing of Heaven.
This speaks of the reality of good and evil,
but not of the effects of suffering and joy.
Jiā ānrén lè,
wealth and resources are sufficient.
Now, being wealthy and abundant
is due to a thick fate;
it is not obtained through virtue and intelligence.
People all know that those who are wealthy, abundant, live peacefully, and are happy have a thick karmic reward,
but they do not know that the state being peaceful and well-governed, and the implementation of [good] transformation is due to a propitious cycle of destiny.
Therefore, a well-governed world is not the achievement of sages and worthies,
and decline and chaos are not the result of the absence of virtue.
When a state is destined for decline and chaos,
sages and worthies cannot make it thrive;
when the time is right for order,
evil people cannot cause chaos.
The order or chaos of the world
depends on the time, not on governance;
the peace or danger of a state
depends on destiny, not on teachings.
Whether a ruler is wise or unwise,
whether policies are clear or unclear,
cannot add to or subtract from [the destiny].
The world praises the time of the Five Emperors,
when the world was at peace,
families had ten years' worth of savings,
and people behaved like gentlemen.
If sometimes it was not so,
the world exaggerates its beauty;
and if sometimes it was so,
It is not caused by governance.
How can this be examined?
The reason why the world is in disorder
is not because of the multitude of bandits and thieves,
the simultaneous rise of armies and weapons,
the people abandoning propriety and righteousness,
and betraying and rebelling against their superiors?
If this is the case,
it is because grains and food are lacking and cut off,
and they cannot endure hunger and cold.
When hunger and cold both arrive, few can avoid wrongdoing.
Therefore, when warmth and fullness both arrive, it is rare for people not to do good.
The *Zhuan* says:
"When the granaries are full,
the people know etiquette;
when clothing and food are sufficient,
the people know honor and shame."
Yielding is born from surplus,
strife arises from deficiency.
When grain is sufficient and food is plentiful,
the heart of propriety and righteousness is born;
when propriety is abundant and righteousness is valued,
the foundation of peace is established.
Therefore, in the spring of a famine year,
one does not feed one's relatives;
in the autumn of a plentiful year,
one summons even one's neighbors.
Not feeding one's relatives
Evil actions;
Summoning and reaching out to the four neighbors is
good and righteous.
The performance of good or evil actions
does not lie in the inherent nature of people,
but depends on the abundance or scarcity of the year.
From this it can be said that
the practice of rites and righteousness
depends on a sufficient grain supply.
Examining the success or failure of grain harvests
is naturally a matter of years and seasons.
In years of drought or flood,
the five grains do not grow,
but this is not caused by government.
It is the natural order of time.
To insist that drought and flood are
caused by government,
there would be no rulers worse than Jié
and Zhòu. In the times of Jié
and Zhòu,
there should have been constant drought and flood.
But in the times of Jié
and Zhòu,
there was no famine or disaster.
Disasters arrive according to a certain order;
sometimes they even occur during the reigns of sage rulers.
Those who speak of actual events cite the floods of Yáo
and the great drought of Tāng;
all were encounters with fate,
and not caused by the wickedness of the government.
To speak of the harm caused by the many kings
and attribute it solely to responses to evil is
to fail to see that Yáo
and Tāng possessed superior virtue.
while the hundred kings were inferior.
Examining one is sufficient to understand a hundred,
and understanding evil is sufficient to illuminate good.
Yáo and Tāng serve as evidence for the hundred kings,
so that when the hundred kings encountered calamities,
it was not caused by governance.
Using observed changes to understand fortune and misfortune,
the five emperors brought about great peace,
not achieved by virtue,
is clear.
When a person dies from a feverish disease,
there are first ominous signs appearing on their face.
Their illness
is encountering a noxious influence.
If their illness does not heal,
and reaches the point of death,
it is because their lifespan is over.
The chaos and downfall of a state
can be verified in the same way.
When there are portents seen in heaven and earth,
it is like a person dying from a feverish disease,
The color appears on the face.
There are calamities of flood and drought,
Just as a person encountering bad qi becomes ill.
If disasters and misfortunes are not removed,
They will lead to the demise of the state,
Just as an illness, if not cured,
Leads to one's death.
Critics say that changes are evidence of misgovernment,
And that the ill complexion of worthy people is ominous.
Can it be said that this is brought about by their conduct?
To say that floods and droughts
Are caused by a lack of virtue,
And that worthy men encounter illness,
Can it be said that this is brought about by their lack of form?
To say that the demise of a state is due to extreme wickedness,
And that the death of worthy men is due to their deeds,
Can it be said that this is due to their great sins?
In fact, worthy men are afflicted by illness and die young,
While wicked men remain strong and live to an old age.
A person's illness and death
Are not due to their conduct or evil deeds.
Therefore, the disorder and demise of a state
Are not due to the rightness or wrongness of its government.
Wicked men remain strong and live to an old age,
It is not because of the peace and stability of the government that it can constantly exist.
From this perspective,
Calamities are insufficient to demonstrate evil,
Auspicious omens are insufficient to represent good,
It is clear.
As for changes in the heavens,
solar and lunar eclipses occur.
Every forty-two months, there is a solar eclipse once;
fifty
six months, there is also a lunar eclipse once.
Eclipses have a constant frequency
and are not dependent on politics.
Hundreds of changes and thousands of calamities
all appear the same;
they are not necessarily caused by the government's governance or teachings.
When Jupiter harms the Bird and Nǔ constellations,
Zhou and Chu face disasters;
when the comet-like gas appears,
Song, Wei,
Chen, and Zheng all experience calamities.
At such times,
the governance and teachings of the six states were not necessarily flawed.
The capital of Lìyáng
sank into a lake overnight;
the officials of Lìyáng at the time were not necessarily deceitful.
Success or failure depends on Heaven;
fortune or misfortune is determined by the timing.
Before human affairs have been initiated,
the weather patterns are already apparent;
what else could it be, if not timing?
The land produces five grains,
Abundance and scarcity;
Grain prices in the market,
One expensive, one cheap.
Abundance does not necessarily mean cheap,
Scarcity does not necessarily mean expensive.
Abundance and scarcity vary with the year,
High and low prices vary with the time.
When the time is right for high prices,
Abundant grain prices increase;
When the time is right for low prices,
Scarce grain prices decrease.
The high and low price of grain does not depend on abundance or scarcity,
Just as the order or disorder of a state does not depend on goodness or evil.
A wise ruler arises,
By chance, in a time when order prevails,
Virtue naturally shines from above,
The people are naturally good below,
The world is peaceful and the people are secure,
Auspicious signs and blessings arrive together,
The world then says that this is brought about by the wise ruler.
A ruler without principle,
By chance, is born in a time when disorder prevails,
The world is disturbed and customs are chaotic,
Disasters are incessant,
Consequently, he destroys the state, loses his life, and extinguishes his line.
The world all says that this is brought about by evil.
Thus,
They are clear about the outward appearance of good and evil,
But do not see the inner reality of fortune and misfortune.
Fortune and misfortune do not depend on goodness or evil,
The proof of goodness and evil does not depend on fortune and misfortune.
When a senior official arrives at his post,
Before he has done anything,
and the governance and teachings remain as before,
with nothing altered or changed,
yet the number of thieves may increase or decrease,
and disasters may or may not occur,
what is the reason for this?
Chief officers of high rank
are entitled to promotion during times of peace and stability;
while those of low station who are deemed incompetent
are subject to demotion and humiliation during times of danger and chaos.
Comparing today's chief officers
to the rulers of ancient states,
their safety, peril, survival, and demise
can be discussed.
*Zìrán Piān* (The Natural Chapter)
When Heaven and Earth combine their *qì*,
all things arise spontaneously,
just as when husband and wife combine their *qì*,
a child is born spontaneously.
The birth of all things,
especially those that contain blood,
is marked by knowing hunger and cold.
Seeing that the five grains can be eaten,
they take them and eat them;
seeing that silk and hemp can be worn,
they take them and wear them.
Some argue that Heaven produces the five grains to feed people
and produces silk and hemp to clothe people.
This would mean that Heaven acts as a farmer
and a silk-reeling woman for people.
This does not accord with nature,
so its meaning is doubtful
and cannot be followed.
Let us try to discuss it according to the Daoist school.
Heaven is that which
universally distributes qi (vital energy) within all things.
Grain alleviates hunger and silk and hemp ward off the cold,
therefore people eat grain
and wear silk and hemp.
That Heaven does not intentionally produce the five grains and silk and hemp to clothe and feed people
is similar to how it does not want to rebuke or warn people through disasters.
Things grow naturally,
and people clothe and feed themselves with them.
Qi changes naturally,
and people fear it.
If we discuss it in this way,
it will satisfy the hearts of the people.
If heavenly omens are intentional,
where is the naturalness?
What is it to dwell in non-action (wú wéi)?
How do we know the naturalness of Heaven?
It is because Heaven has no mouth or eyes.
Considering those with action (yǒu wéi),
They are of the kind with mouths and eyes.
The mouth desires to eat, and the eyes desire to see,
Having desires and wants within,
They are manifested externally,
Mouths and eyes seek them,
Gaining them as benefit;
This is the action (wéi) of desire.
Now, lacking the desires of mouths and eyes,
With nothing sought or demanded from things,
What action (wéi) would there be?
How do we know Heaven has no mouths or eyes?
We know it by observing the Earth.
The Earth takes soil as its substance,
Soil inherently has no mouths or eyes.
Heaven and Earth
are like husband and wife.
The Earth's substance has no mouths or eyes,
Therefore, we also know that Heaven has no mouths or eyes.
If Heaven has substance (tǐ),
it should be the same as the Earth.
If it's the *qi* of Heaven,
*Qi* is like clouds and smoke,
Belonging to the category of clouds and smoke,
How could it have mouths and eyes?
Someone asked:
"All things that move and act
are fundamentally without intention.
Because there is desire, there is movement;
when there is movement, there is action.
Now, the movement of Heaven is similar to that of humans,
how can it be said to be without intention?"
I reply: The movement of Heaven
is the emanation of *qì*
when the body moves, *qì* comes forth,
and things are born.
It is similar to how humans move *qì*:
when the body moves, *qì* comes forth,
and children are born.
When humans emanate *qì*,
it is not with the intention of producing children,
but when *qì* emanates, children are born naturally.
Heaven's movement is not with the intention of producing things,
but things are born naturally.
This is what is meant by *zìrán* (naturalness).
The emanation of *qì* is not done with the intention of creating things,
but things create themselves.
This is what is meant by *wúwéi* (non-action).
What is meant by saying that Heaven is naturally without intention (*zìrán wúwéi*)?
It is *qì*.
Being tranquil, serene, and without desire,
without intention and without affairs,
Lǎodān was able to live a long life.
Lǎodān received this from Heaven,
If Heaven did not have this *qì*,
from where could Lǎo Dān have received this nature?
That a disciple alone should speak of something that the teacher has no explanation for,
there has never been such a thing.
Someone reported to Duke Huán,
and the Duke said:
"Tell Zhòngfǔ."
Those around him said:
"First Zhòngfǔ,
second Zhòngfǔ,
is being a ruler so easy!"
Duke Huán said:
"I have not yet obtained Zhòngfǔ,
therefore it is difficult;
having already obtained Zhòngfǔ,
why would it not be easy?"
Duke Huán obtained Zhòngfǔ,
entrusted him with affairs,
delegated political power to him,
and no longer concerned himself with knowledge.
If August Heaven, with its supremely excellent virtue,
were to follow royal policies and send warnings of condemnation,
then Heaven's virtue would not be as good as Duke Huán's,
and the conduct of a hegemonic ruler would surpass that of God on High.
Someone said:
"Huán Gōng knew that Guǎn Zhòng was virtuous,
therefore he entrusted him with responsibilities;
if it were not Guǎn Zhòng,
he would have also reproached and warned him.
If Heaven had encountered Yáo and
Shùn, there would certainly be no incident of reproach and warning."
Someone said: If Heaven can reproach and warn a ruler,
then it can also deliberately appoint a sage ruler,
select talent like Yáo and
Shùn, bestow upon them the Mandate of Heaven,
entrust them with royal affairs,
and not interfere again.
But now it is not so,
it produces mediocre rulers,
who lose the Way and abandon virtue,
and then it reproaches and warns them,
why is Heaven not afraid of being troubled?
Cáo Shēn, as the chancellor of Hàn,
indulged in wine, songs, and entertainment,
and did not attend to governmental affairs.
When his son advised him,
he flogged him two hundred times.
At that time, there were no disturbances or rebellions in the empire.
In Huáiyáng, they minted counterfeit coins,
and the officials could not stop it.
Jí Àn became the governor,
he did not destroy a single furnace,
nor did he punish a single person,
Sleeping soundly with a high pillow,
yet Huáiyáng was governed with clarity.
Cáo Cān as chancellor
acted as if he were not chancellor.
Jí Àn as grand administrator
acted as if the commandery had no one.
Yet the Hàn dynasty was without incident,
and in Huáiyáng punishments were rarely applied,
because Cān's virtue was superior and Àn's authority weighty.
Considering the majesty and virtue of Heaven,
how do they compare with Cáo Cān and
Jí Àn?
To say that Heaven monitors the king's government
and sends down warnings accordingly
is to say that Heaven's virtue is not as profound as Cáo Cān's,
and its authority not as weighty as Jí Àn's.
Qū Bóyù governing Wèi,
Zǐ Gòng sent someone to ask him:
"How do you govern Wèi?"
He replied:
"I govern it by not governing it."
Governing by not governing
is the Dao of non-action.
Some say:
"As a response to great peace,
the Hé River produces a chart,
the Luò River produces a scroll.
Not painted, not accomplished;
not done, not achieved.

"Discerning Calamities"
Common customs believe in misfortune and calamities,
thinking that people's illnesses, deaths,
and even suffering disasters and being punished,
humiliation and laughter,

Commencing construction,
moving house,
conducting sacrifices,
holding funerals,
performing work,
entering officialdom,

not avoiding the year,
or the month, encountering ghosts and meeting spirits,
with inauspicious times harming each other.
Therefore, falling ill and suffering misfortune,
being ensnared by the law and committing crimes,
even to the point of death,
exhausting the family and exterminating the clan,
all because of not being cautious,
and violating taboos.
If truthfully discussed,
it is but baseless talk.
All people in the world
cannot avoid doing things,
and after doing things,
cannot avoid having good or bad fortune.
When good fortune is seen, they point to it as the blessing of choosing an auspicious day in the past.
When misfortune is seen, they blame it on having violated a taboo in the past.
Often, people choose auspicious days and still encounter misfortune,
or violate taboos and obtain blessings.
The artisans and technicians who practice these arts want to achieve their goals,
Seeing calamity and resenting it without speaking,
hearing of blessings and concealing them without communicating them,
accumulating calamities to startle the incautious,
arranging blessings to encourage those who fear the times.
Therefore, people in the world, whether foolish or wise,
virtuous or unworthy,
rulers or commoners,
